stories.headline: House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker; seven newcomers say they voted no
stories.summary: House Democrats chose Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday as their nominee for speaker in the new Congress, which takes office in January. The vote was by secret ballot, but seven incoming Democratic members said publicly that they voted against him. The full House still has to elect the speaker when it convenes.
stories.why_it_matters: The speaker decides which bills reach the House floor, so Jeffries would shape what Democrats try to pass, from spending bills to investigations of the Trump administration, after the party takes control in January.
stories.background: Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Jeffries, a Brooklyn congressman, has led House Democrats since 2023, when he succeeded Nancy Pelosi, and has been the minority leader under Republican control. Some progressives and activist groups had pushed incoming members not to back him, arguing the party needs new leadership, while supporters point to the election results. If elected by the full House, he would be the first Black speaker.

facts.text: House Democrats nominated Jeffries for speaker on Wednesday, Nov. 18, in a secret-ballot caucus vote.
Seven incoming members of the House Democratic Caucus said publicly that they voted against his nomination, NBC News reported; The Washington Post put the number at at least seven progressives.
If the full House elects him in January, Jeffries would be the first Black speaker of the House.
Jeffries told Democrats their job was to fight what he called "Maga extremism" rather than each other, according to The Guardian.
NPR reported that Democrats are also preparing investigations into the Trump administration to begin once they take control in January.
In the week after the midterms, some progressives argued Jeffries was not the right person for the job, TheGrio reported.

stories.headline: Justice Department widens 'Decoy Dan' probe as Alaska prepares to certify Peltola's win
stories.summary: A day after Democrat Mary Peltola was declared the winner of Alaska's Senate race, Fox News reported that the Justice Department has issued about 200 subpoenas in a criminal probe tied to the candidacy of a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot. The result is scheduled to be certified next week. In Alaska's House race, Republican Rep. Nick Begich won a second term.
stories.why_it_matters: The probe could become the basis for Republican challenges to a seat that gives Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority, though no court has questioned the count.
stories.background: Peltola beat Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in a ranked-choice race that also included Dan J. Sullivan, a former schoolteacher with the same name. The Justice Department opened a criminal investigation and also sued to block certification, a suit a federal judge dismissed. The Alaska Supreme Court had ruled that Dan J. Earlier, prosecutors issued grand jury subpoenas, including to Peltola's campaign, as they examined whether getting Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot violated federal conspiracy laws, ABC News reported.
Peltola's win gave Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority and their ninth flipped seat, their biggest midterm Senate gain in nearly 70 years.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin hold first three-way summit in Shenzhen
stories.summary: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia met together for the first time on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The meeting lasted about an hour and 20 minutes. Russia said the three agreed there can be no winners in a nuclear war and that they would boost oil and gas production, but no detailed agreement had been published by the time early coverage ran.
stories.why_it_matters: The three countries hold most of the world's nuclear weapons and are tied up in the wars in Ukraine and with Iran, which affect energy prices and global security. Early reports describe statements of principle, not a deal.
stories.background: Russia, China and the United States have never before held a three-way leaders' meeting. Putin first proposed the format in an October call with Trump, and the White House confirmed the plan days before the APEC gathering in Shenzhen. Trump has pushed for the three powers to cut their nuclear stockpiles, while Beijing has long refused to join trilateral arms-control talks. The meeting came during the war in Ukraine and the US-Iran conflict that began with US and Israeli strikes in February.

facts.text: Trump told the other two leaders that they were "really making history" as the meeting opened.

Before the three-way meeting, Trump told Xi that the US and China should both help end the war in Ukraine, Reuters reported.
Trump said the US, China and Russia were "uniquely positioned" to discuss reducing nuclear weapons.
The White House announced the meeting on Nov. 14 as an unprecedented joint session on the sidelines of APEC.

stories.headline: World Court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed acts of genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during military operations in 2017. The court said Myanmar's forces killed thousands of Rohingya and that the state intended to destroy a substantial part of the group. The case, brought by The Gambia, has been followed closely because of South Africa's genocide case against Israel.
stories.why_it_matters: It is a rare ruling by the UN's top court that a state committed genocide, and how the court read the legal test of intent could shape other cases, including the one over Gaza. For about a million Rohingya refugees, it is a formal finding about what happened to them.
stories.background: In 2017 Myanmar's military carried out what it called clearance operations in Rakhine state, and hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. In 2019 The Gambia, backed by other Muslim-majority countries, sued Myanmar at the International Court of Justice under the Genocide Convention. Myanmar denied the charge and said the operations targeted militants. Hearings on the merits took place in January 2026, and the judgment is final, with no appeal.

facts.text: The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed acts of genocide against the Rohingya during the 2017 operations.
The court found that Myanmar's forces killed thousands of Rohingya, Reuters reported while the ruling was being read.
The court said Myanmar intended to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population, and that soldiers killed and raped Rohingya, committed violence against children and destroyed villages.
The Gambia brought the case after the 2017 crackdown, and proving intent to destroy a group was the key legal test.
Observers are watching the ruling for what it could mean for South Africa's genocide case against Israel over Gaza.
The judgment is final and cannot be appealed, according to Human Rights Watch; Myanmar has said its operations were a counter-terrorism campaign.

stories.headline: Iran strikes at US base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain after US hits Qeshm Island
stories.summary: Iran targeted a US air base in Kuwait and several sites in Bahrain on Wednesday, a day after US forces struck Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait said its air defenses intercepted drones. On Thursday the International Energy Agency said the Middle East crisis is the largest threat to energy security in history.
stories.why_it_matters: Renewed fighting around the Strait of Hormuz keeps pressure on oil and gas supplies, and the IEA says consumers are increasingly absorbing the cost through higher prices.
stories.background: The US and Israel struck Iran in February, starting a war that has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route for a large share of the world's oil. A ceasefire in April reduced the fighting, but both sides have traded strikes since, including a similar round in June involving Qeshm Island, Kuwait and Bahrain. Peace talks have stalled. Gulf states that host US forces, such as Kuwait and Bahrain, have been caught in the middle.

facts.text: Iran targeted the Ali Al Salem air base used by US forces in Kuwait and launched attacks on Bahrain on Wednesday.
The Iranian strikes followed US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
Kuwait said it repelled the attack, its first from Iran in two months, and that its air defenses intercepted drones.
Before the US strikes, Iran had attacked US radar systems in Bahrain three times in less than a week, CBS News reported.
Iran had also set a natural gas tanker on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The International Energy Agency said the crisis is the largest threat to energy security in history and that consumers and high prices are increasingly absorbing the impact.
A similar exchange took place in June, when US strikes on Qeshm Island were followed by Iranian fire at Kuwait and Bahrain.

stories.headline: Crimean Bridge attacked for third time in days, halting trains
stories.summary: Ukraine struck the rail section of the Kerch (Crimean) Bridge overnight, its third attack in four days, and train traffic between Russia and occupied Crimea was halted, according to Crimea's Russian-installed governor. Earlier strikes this week destroyed part of the bridge's road section. The attack came hours before Putin's summit with Trump and Xi in China.
stories.why_it_matters: The bridge is a main supply route for Russian forces and residents in Crimea, so cutting it raises pressure on Russia while leaders talk about ending the war. Ukraine's parallel strikes on refineries also affect Russian fuel exports.
stories.background: Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014 and opened the 19-kilometer road and rail bridge across the Kerch Strait in 2018. It is seen as a symbol of Putin's rule and a key military supply line. Ukraine has attacked it several times since the 2022 invasion, including a truck bomb that year and a strike in 2023. This week Ukraine hit it on Nov. 16 and 17, and again overnight into Nov. 19.

The Nov. 17 strike killed two people, governor Sergei Aksyonov said, and road traffic stayed closed while ferries carried vehicles.
Russia has vowed to restore the bridge quickly, but engineering specialists say repairs could take years, The New York Times reported.
Ukraine's General Staff said it struck two oil refineries in Russia's Krasnodar region on Nov. 18.
Reuters, citing two industry sources, reported that Ukrainian attacks over 20 days disrupted or stopped 15 of Russia's 35 major refineries, cutting processing by about 45%.

stories.headline: Denmark ratifies Greenland security deal with the US
stories.summary: Denmark's parliament on Thursday unanimously approved a security agreement with Greenland and the United States that expands US military access on the Arctic island. The vote was the last step needed for the deal to take effect. It follows months of tension after President Trump said the US should take control of Greenland.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal settles, for now, a dispute between the US and a NATO ally that had raised fears of a split in the alliance, and it gives the US a bigger military footprint in the Arctic.
stories.background: Greenland is a semi-autonomous territory of Denmark with a population of about 57,000 and a strategic position between North America and Europe. The US already runs the Pituffik Space Base there under a 1951 agreement. Trump repeatedly said the US should control Greenland and did not rule out force, which strained relations with Denmark. The three governments signed a security agreement to end the standoff, and Greenland's own parliament approved it earlier in November.

stories.headline: Israeli forces cross Gaza ceasefire line in first raid since truce
stories.summary: Israeli tanks crossed the "Yellow Line" into Hamas-held central Gaza on Wednesday, the first ground operation across that boundary since the ceasefire, and Israel said on Thursday the raid had ended. stories.why_it_matters: The raid tests a fragile ceasefire that has largely halted full-scale war in Gaza, where Palestinians still face severe shortages of food and shelter.
stories.background: A ceasefire between Israel and Hamas took effect in October 2025. It created a boundary called the Yellow Line, with Israeli troops pulling back to it but still holding part of the Gaza Strip, and Hamas controlling the rest. Both sides have accused each other of violations since. Israeli politics are also in flux, with Gadi Eisenkot trying to form a government without Benjamin Netanyahu, according to The Guardian.

stories.headline: UN watchdog says North Korea is expanding its Yongbyon enrichment plant
stories.summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency said North Korea is expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at the Yongbyon nuclear complex. stories.background: North Korea has tested nuclear weapons six times and is under UN sanctions for its weapons programs. Yongbyon is its main nuclear site, and the IAEA, which has had no inspectors in the country since 2009, monitors it through satellite imagery. Earlier this year the agency reported a new enrichment building at Yongbyon and activity at a second enrichment site, Kangson. South Korea's Lee has sought to reopen dialogue with Pyongyang.

stories.headline: Fed minutes show officials expect to raise rates again in December
stories.summary: Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October meeting, released Wednesday, show nearly all officials expect to raise the benchmark interest rate by a quarter point in December, with some having wanted a hike in October already. The dollar rose to its highest level in about 19 months and gold slipped as traders priced in more tightening. The Fed's next decision comes at its December meeting.
stories.why_it_matters: Another rate increase would push up borrowing costs on credit cards, car loans and new adjustable-rate debt, while savers could see slightly higher yields on deposits.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve sets a short-term interest rate that steers borrowing costs across the economy, raising it to cool inflation and cutting it to support growth. In 2026 the Fed has been raising rates as an energy shock tied to the Iran war, tariffs and heavy spending on AI data centers kept prices elevated. At its October 28 meeting it held the rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%, a decision that was not unanimous. Minutes are a detailed summary of the meeting, published about three weeks later, and markets read them for hints about the next move.

facts.text: At its October meeting the Fed held its benchmark rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%.
The minutes show nearly all officials expect a quarter-point increase in December; some supported a hike in October, and two raised the possibility of a half-point increase.
A "vast majority" of officials worried inflation could persist even if gas prices kept falling and the effects of tariffs and the AI infrastructure buildout faded, the minutes show.
Officials discussed the effect of AI-related spending on inflation, CNBC reported.
Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented from the October decision.
The WSJ Dollar Index rose to a new 52-week high after the minutes were released, and the dollar held near a 19-month high on Thursday as Treasury yields rose.
Gold futures slipped to about $3,737 an ounce on Thursday, with the Wall Street Journal attributing the decline to bets on further rate hikes.

stories.headline: Nvidia's interim CEO tells staff to move on from Huang as the stock keeps falling
stories.summary: Interim CEO Colette Kress told Nvidia employees at the first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang's resignation to "move forward" and offered pay raises, according to reports. The meeting followed quarterly results showing revenue up 103%, but the stock fell again on Wednesday, while investor Bill Ackman criticized the board for pushing Huang out. The board is searching for a permanent CEO.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the largest companies in the stock market, so its slide weighs on the index funds and 401(k)s many people hold.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the chips that power most AI systems and became the world's most valuable company during the AI boom. Co-founder Jensen Huang ran it for 33 years until he resigned as CEO and director on November 12; the company's announcement did not give a reason, and reporting has tied his exit to revelations about his personal conduct. The board named finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO and Harvey Jones chair. The stock had already lost a large share of its value from an October peak before the resignation.

facts.text: Nvidia announced on November 12 that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, CEO and director, effective immediately, and named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO.
Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, and forecast about $130 billion for the next quarter.
At a company all-hands meeting, Kress urged employees to "move forward" and offered pay raises.
The New York Post, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Kress sought to discourage calls for Huang's return.
Investor Bill Ackman said the board "rushed to judgment" and did not act in the best interest of the company, customers or shareholders.
OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anduril's Palmer Luckey expressed support for Huang at the DealBook Summit, The New York Times reported.
Nvidia shares fell again on Wednesday as the company's efforts failed to stabilize the stock or ease concerns about its "neocloud" customers, the Wall Street Journal reported.

stories.headline: IEA says Iran war's energy shock will permanently change energy use
stories.summary: The International Energy Agency said in its annual outlook that there is no return to the energy system that existed before the Iran war, and that countries' energy-security responses could cut oil demand by 4% by 2035. The report comes as attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue and high fuel prices push up inflation, including in Britain.
stories.why_it_matters: The war has kept gasoline and diesel prices high, and the IEA's view suggests the shift toward other energy sources that drivers and households are seeing will last.
stories.background: The International Energy Agency is a Paris-based body that advises mostly wealthy countries on energy. The war involving Iran has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passage for a large share of the world's oil, causing an oil price shock in 2026. Earlier this year the IEA said global oil demand would fall for the first time since the pandemic. Its annual outlook is its most comprehensive look at where energy use is heading.

facts.text: The IEA said the energy-security response to the Iran war could cut oil demand by 4% by 2035.

The New York Times reported that the IEA found the oil shock could speed the adoption of alternative power sources.
Iran has continued attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, including a strike on an already disabled vessel, The New York Times reported.

stories.headline: City will tear down building next to deadly Flatbush collapse
stories.summary: The city Department of Buildings said Wednesday evening that 1323 Flatbush Avenue, the apartment building beside last week's fatal collapse, is too unstable to repair and will be demolished. Inspectors are also reviewing about 160 construction sites tied to the contractors working next to the collapsed building, and The New York Times obtained video from an MTA bus that shows the moments before the building fell.
stories.why_it_matters: Residents of the damaged neighboring building lose their homes for good, and the citywide sweep of sites linked to the same contractors could pause construction near many New Yorkers' homes. Follow-up coverage in the digest comes from left-leaning and center outlets plus the right-leaning New York Post.
stories.background: Last week a three-story apartment building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a construction site next door, killing eight people, including two children. The Department of Buildings had issued a stop-work order at the neighboring demolition site earlier this year and later lifted it, and city records showed a cracked facade had been flagged months before the collapse. Mayor Zohran Mamdani ordered an emergency review of other jobs run by the firms involved. The official cause of the collapse has not yet been determined.

stories.headline: Man accused of three Central Park rapes appears in Manhattan court
stories.summary: Dereck Rivera-Deleon, arrested in Miami Beach and extradited to New York, appeared in Manhattan court Wednesday on rape charges tied to attacks near Central Park dating back to 2021. After an attack in late October, the NYPD circulated the suspect's picture, and Rivera-Deleon was arrested in Miami Beach on Nov. 10 in an operation with the U.S. Marshals Service. He was held in Florida pending extradition and has now been brought back to New York to face charges.

stories.headline: MTA moves to fire nine bus fare inspectors after clashes with riders
stories.summary: MTA officials brought disciplinary charges against nine members of the EAGLE Team, the unit that checks bus fares, and recommended that all nine be fired after an investigation into two violent incidents with riders. The unit's work was already halted in October.
stories.why_it_matters: The case shapes how, and whether, the MTA polices fare evasion on city buses, which affects everyday interactions between riders and transit staff.
stories.background: The MTA's Evasion and Graffiti Lawlessness Eradication (EAGLE) Teams were created to check fares on buses, especially on routes with all-door boarding. In October, videos of two separate scuffles between agents and riders in which agents appeared to use force drew attention, and the MTA pulled the teams from the bus system pending a review. An internal investigation found the conduct violated agency policy, and some progressive City Council members called for the squads to be eliminated.

stories.headline: Mamdani plan would start demolishing a Rikers jail in 2027
stories.summary: The Mamdani administration plans to begin tearing down a jail on Rikers Island next year, starting with a nearly century-old jail and medical facility, as part of a new blueprint to close the complex, THE CITY reported. The city is not expected to meet its legal 2027 deadline to close Rikers entirely.
stories.why_it_matters: Closing Rikers is tied to building borough jails and lowering the jail population, decisions that affect public safety, city spending and the neighborhoods slated for new jails. The demolition plan itself was reported by one center outlet; the Daily News weighed in with an opinion piece.
stories.background: Rikers Island, the city's main jail complex in the East River, has long faced criticism over violence and deaths in custody. In 2019 the City Council passed a law to close it by August 2027 and replace it with four smaller jails in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx. Construction delays and a jail population above the new jails' capacity have put that deadline out of reach. Mayor Zohran Mamdani supported the closure during his campaign, while rival Andrew Cuomo proposed rebuilding on the island instead.

stories.headline: MTA says chronic sick calls by bus drivers cost riders 120,000 trips
stories.summary: MTA officials said Wednesday that close to 1,000 bus operators call out sick more than 50 days a year, and they blamed those absences for nearly 120,000 canceled bus trips so far this year, THE CITY reported.

stories.background: New York City Transit runs one of the largest bus fleets in the country, and missed trips due to too few available drivers have been a recurring problem. Sick leave for bus operators is set by contracts with the Transport Workers Union. MTA leaders have been focused on bus reliability while also dealing with the fare enforcement controversy.

stories.headline: MTA outlines plans to raise fares again
stories.summary: The MTA plans to raise fares on subways and buses, the LIRR and Metro-North, the Daily News reported, less than a year after the base fare rose to $3. The size and timing of the increase were not in the early report.
stories.why_it_matters: Another fare increase would raise the cost of daily commuting for millions of riders. The story was covered by a single left-leaning outlet in the digest.
stories.background: The MTA raises fares and tolls about every two years to help balance its operating budget. The subway and bus base fare went to $3 in January 2026 after a board vote in 2025. The agency's financial plan has called for further increases in 2027 and 2029. Fare changes require public hearings and a vote by the MTA board.

markets.summary: U.S. stocks ended Wednesday mixed: the Dow fell 1.1% and the S&P 500 slipped 0.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq gained 0.4%. Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October meeting showed nearly all officials expect to raise interest rates by a quarter point in December to fight inflation, which was 3.7% in September; that pushed the dollar near a 19-month high and pulled gold lower. Nvidia's shares fell again despite revenue that roughly doubled from a year earlier, as investors weighed the departure of chief executive Jensen Huang. Stock futures rose overnight ahead of Anthropic's record-sized stock market debut on Thursday, seen as a test of how much investors will pay for artificial intelligence companies. The 10-year Treasury yield, a benchmark for mortgages and other loans, stays near 5.1%, keeping the average 30-year mortgage rate above 7%.

movers.why: Bitcoin fell another 2.2% and is down about 23% over the past month; today's coverage doesn't give a clear cause, though it has fallen alongside other risky assets as rate-hike expectations rose.

concept.explanation: A rate hike is when the Federal Reserve raises its benchmark interest rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed raises it to cool inflation: when borrowing costs more, people and businesses spend less, which eases pressure on prices. A quarter-point hike, the step most officials now expect in December, adds 0.25 percentage point. Banks usually lift credit card and home equity rates within weeks, and savings accounts tend to pay a bit more, while mortgage rates often move earlier, as soon as investors expect the hike.
